question.text: Sortino Ratio improves upon Sharpe by:

answer.text: Using total risk including upside volatility
Using only downside deviation instead of total standard deviation, focusing on harmful volatility
Using beta instead of standard deviation

explanation.text: The Logic: The Sortino Ratio = (Return - Target Return) / Downside Deviation. Unlike the Sharpe Ratio, which uses total standard deviation in the denominator, Sortino uses only the downside deviation — the standard deviation of returns falling below a target/minimum-acceptable return. This isolates harmful volatility and ignores beneficial upside volatility, giving a cleaner risk-adjusted-return signal for asymmetric-return portfolios. The Trap: "Using total risk including upside volatility" describes Sharpe, not the improvement Sortino makes. "Ignoring risk entirely" is incorrect — Sortino still measures risk, just selectively. "Using beta instead of standard deviation" describes Treynor, not Sortino. Note: The cited NISM Series XV Research Analyst workbook pages reviewed in the audit cover standard deviation, the Sharpe Ratio, and the Treynor Ratio but do not contain a definition of the Sortino Ratio or downside deviation on the pages checked. The framing above reflects general industry/regulatory knowledge of risk-adjusted return measures.
